question: Is organ donation halal, and can I register as a donor on my driver's license form?
asked: Somebody was filling out his driver's license form, got to the question of organ donation and got stuck. What should he do? Is organ donation halal in Islam?
answer:
> وَمَا أَرْسَلْنَا مِن قَبْلِكَ إِلَّا رِجَالًا نُّوحِي إِلَيْهِمْ فَاسْأَلُوا أَهْلَ الذِّكْرِ إِن كُنتُمْ لَا تَعْلَمُونَ

Last year, the Fiqh Council discussed this in our annual meeting, and we released our fatwa about organ donation. The Fiqh Council of North America, as you should all know, is the senior-most and eldest body. It was formed in the early 1980s, and it is a council that deals with modern issues and fatwas. It is headed by some esteemed scholars, including Dr. Muzammil Siddiqi, Dr. Zulfiqar Ali, Dr. Jamal Badawi and Dr. Jasser Auda. I'm also one of the junior members on the council.

So we discussed this issue of organ donation and we released a fatwa about it. We said that there are certain areas that are, inshallah, very clearly halal, other areas that are very clearly haram, and, as usual, there's a bit of a grey area.

As for the clear halal, what is without a doubt acceptable is that a person donates an organ to another person. It is not a requirement that the person be Muslim. **You may donate an organ to another person that is needed for the life or the stability of the other person, as long as the first person does not give his life up for the other person.** You don't kill yourself for the other person.

So the person can write in his will: when I die, you may give my heart to somebody who needs it; you may give my liver to somebody who needs it. While alive, you may donate that which you can live without, like your kidney. I don't think there's anything else, maybe half of a liver, whatever; the doctors know best. But whatever you can live without, you may give to a person who needs it to live a normal life, or to live a life.

But you cannot give for the sake of money. You cannot sell your organs. **By unanimous consensus, it is haram to sell your organs.** It is haram to give blood for a gift. You do not give blood to get money. Why? Because our body does not belong to us. It belongs to Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala. We cannot sell what we don't own. I don't own my body; Allah owns my body.

I can sell what I own. I can sell you my iPhone. I cannot sell you my kidney. I cannot sell you my blood. I cannot sell you my organs. It is haram to buy and sell one's organs. So you may donate your organs to another human being.

However, to donate to what is called science, the Fiqh Council said no, because this is a type of mutilation: to simply cut up a body and open things up and look at them. Our Prophet ﷺ said (the hadith is in Abu Dawud): breaking the bones of a corpse is as sinful as breaking the bones of a living person. This is a hadith. And our Prophet ﷺ forbade mutilation, even of the pagan enemies in the Battle of Badr. He forbade mutilation. And cutting up the body and taking things out, this is a type of mutilation.

So we do not do this to ourselves willingly. We do not do it to our loved ones. And that's why, as well, autopsies: we try our best not to do them. If the government requires it, it requires it, but we don't willingly just do it for no reason. We want to protect the sanctity of the body.

As well, by unanimous consensus of all the fiqh councils of the world, reproductive organs cannot be donated. You cannot donate male or female reproductive organs; this is something that is not allowed.

As well, the person whose organ is donated is the person who must sign in his will or her will that 'I want my organs to be donated.'

Now, the grey area. What if the person didn't say yes or no? If the person said yes or no, that's binding. What if he was quiet? Then the heirs come and say, 'Our cousin needs his liver,' 'Our sister needs this,' and the heirs decide to take an organ. There's a bit of a grey area. The Fiqh Council allowed this: if the heirs unanimously agree, and they feel that our brother, our father, our mother would willingly give up an organ to such and such a person, and if they agree, then inshallah it is allowed to do that. If they don't unanimously agree, then that's one of those grey areas.

And the biggest area where we did not and could not reach a decisive verdict, because doctors themselves have not reached a decisive verdict, is: when does death begin and life end, such that you may take the organ out? I'm not a medical doctor, but from what I understand, there is this small gap with a person who's about to die, where you need to take the heart or the liver or the kidney at a time when technically the heart's still beating, but the brain might be dead, for example. So you need to take it out, and you're going to cause the death of this patient. This was a grey area, because doctors themselves have not quite fine-tuned this.

For sure, if the patient has died, you may take the organs out, if he said you may take them out. But what if the patient is on that line between life and death? Can you take an organ that will cause the death, knowing that he's about to die? This is something that doctors themselves are discussing amongst themselves. So the Fiqh Council said, we need to come back and look at this when we have more information. That is the only grey area that was there in this regard.
